sections.abstract: The paper addresses the lack of foundation models in 3D, specifically for object part segmentation, due to data scarcity. Existing datasets are small and lack diversity. The authors introduce FIND3D, the first general-category 3D model capable of segmenting any part of any object using any text query. This is achieved through a scalable Data Engine powered by 2D foundation models (SAM and Gemini) that automatically annotates 3D assets from the web. The engine generates $1755\times$ more unique part types than all existing datasets combined. By training a transformer-based point cloud model with a contrastive objective on this data, the authors obtain an open-world model that generalizes to any part in any object. FIND3D achieves a $260\%$ improvement in mIoU and boosts inference speed by $6\times$ to $300\times$ compared to existing methods, even when evaluated zero-shot. The authors also release a new benchmark for general-category open-world 3D part segmentation.
sections.introduction: The introduction explores the possibility of building 3D foundation models similar to those in text and image modalities. The primary challenge is the absence of internet-scale 3D datasets. The authors demonstrate that a strong model can be built using a simple, general training recipe if the data challenge is addressed. FIND3D unlocks generalization to unseen objects with a $260\%$ improvement in mIoU and outperforms prior methods on their own training datasets. Prior works often relied on dataset-specific customizations and small, homogeneous datasets like ShapeNet-Part (16 categories), which hindered generalization. The goals of this paper are to establish a scalable data engine and show that large-scale training enables strong generalization without specific customizations.
sections.method:
The paper categorizes related work into four areas: 1) Closed-world 3D segmentation, which is often domain-specific and limited to whole objects or coarse granularity (e.g., ShapeNet-Part with 16 categories or PartNet-E with 45). 2) 3D aggregation methods based on 2D renderings, which use models like CLIP, SAM, or GLIP to assemble 3D understanding from multiview renderings. These methods often lack 3D geometry information and are slow due to multiple inferences at test time. 3) Test-time optimization, which combines 2D features with 3D representations like NeRF or Gaussian Splatting (e.g., LERF, Garfield). These are slow as they require per-scene optimization. 4) Distillation methods, which train 3D models using 2D annotations but are typically limited to specific datasets or categories, hindering zero-shot generalization. The authors propose FIND3D to locate any object part in 3D based on free-form language descriptions. Given a point cloud $C = \{p_1, ...p_n\}$ where each point $p_i = (x, y, z, n_x, n_y, n_z, r, g, b) \in \mathbb{R}^9$, the model predicts a semantic feature $f_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ in the latent space of a CLIP-like model (SigLIP). At inference, for any text $s$, the model computes cosine similarity $\cos(T(s), f_i)$ to segment parts.

**Data Engine:** The engine leverages SAM and Gemini to annotate Objaverse assets. Gemini selects the best orientation from 10 renderings, SAM generates 2D masks with gridpoint prompts, and Gemini names the shaded parts. Masks are back-projected to 3D points. The engine processed 36,044 objects, yielding 2.1M part annotations and 124,615 unique part types ($1775\times$ more than existing datasets).

**Open-World 3D Part Model:** The architecture uses PT3, treating point clouds as sequences. A 4-layer MLP aligns point features to the 768-dimension SigLIP space. The model has 46.2M parameters. Training uses a contrastive loss to handle partial labels and ambiguity. For a label $(C_i, T(\text{label}_i))$, the pooled feature $f(C_i)$ is the average feature of points in $C_i$. The loss is defined as:
$l_i = - \log \frac{\exp(f(C_i) \cdot T(\text{label}_i))}{\sum_{j=1}^{|B|} \exp(f(C_i) \cdot T(\text{label}_j))}$ (1)
where $B$ denotes all labels in a batch. Training uses a batch size of 64 objects and various data augmentations (rotation, scaling, jittering).
sections.experiments: Existing benchmarks are limited to narrow domains and few categories. The authors introduce a new benchmark divided into two sets: 1) Objaverse-General, containing 100 objects with 350 parts from 100 diverse categories (e.g., gondola, easel, penguin) in random orientations. 50 categories are held out for unseen evaluation. 2) ShapeNetPart-V2, containing 32 objects from the same 16 categories as ShapeNet-Part but sourced from Objaverse to test domain generalization. The benchmark features $5\times$ more unique part types and $2.9\times$ more object categories than previous benchmarks. FIND3D is compared against open-world baselines (PointCLIPV2, PartSLIP++, OpenMask3D) and closed-world baselines (PointNeXt, PartDistill). FIND3D is the only method that is simultaneously open-world, cross-category, part-level, and feed-forward.
sections.results:
It achieves a $260\%$ improvement in mIoU on unseen categories compared to the best baseline. It is $6\times$ to $300\times$ faster than other open-world models, taking only 0.9s for inference.

**Scaling Analysis:** A strong scaling trend is observed; increasing training object categories from 16 to 761 significantly improves zero-shot mIoU on Objaverse-Unseen categories.

**Robustness:** FIND3D is robust to variations in query prompts and object orientation. While PointCLIPV2's performance drops by $64\%$ when changing prompts, FIND3D remains stable. It also handles domain shifts better, showing a $1.5\times$ advantage over PointNeXt on ShapeNetPart-V2.

**Flexibility and Failure Modes:** The model supports flexible queries (e.g., 'hand' vs 'gloves') and varying granularities ('limbs' vs 'arms'). Limitations include difficulty with fine-grained, non-geometrically prominent parts (e.g., buttons) due to voxel-sampling resolution (0.02) and a tendency toward symmetric predictions due to rotational equivariance.
sections.conclusion: The paper presents the first scaling study for 3D part segmentation. The key contribution is a data engine that automatically annotates internet-scale 3D assets, enabling the training of a zero-shot generalist model. The results underscore that training diversity is critical for generalization. The authors plan to release their code, benchmark, and model checkpoints to encourage the community to move toward large-scale, general-category 3D understanding.
sections.supplementary:
The supplementary material provides additional details and qualitative results. 

**Additional Data Engine Examples:** Manual inspection of 50 random objects showed $76\%$ high-quality annotations. Lower-quality examples often involve objects without pronounced parts (e.g., baguette) or incorrect labels that the model can 'smooth out' during large-scale training. 

**Additional Qualitative Results:** Figures show FIND3D's predictions on Objaverse-General, PartObjaverse-Tiny, and real-world iPhone photos reconstructed to 3D using Trellis. The model generalizes well to real-world data despite being trained on synthetic assets.

**Additional Results:** Full-set evaluation results on ShapeNet-Part and PartNet-E are provided. FIND3D performs best in 8 out of 9 configurations on ShapeNet-Part and is over $30\times$ faster than PartSLIP++ on PartNet-E while being more robust to prompt variations.

**Data Engine Prompts:** The document details the specific prompts used for Gemini. For orientation selection, Gemini is asked if an object is in a 'usually seen' orientation based on 10 renderings. For part naming, Gemini is asked to name a part masked in purple as a single word or phrase.
